cycloastragenol.summary: A purified astragalus compound sold as a telomerase activator so skin and vitality age more slowly; research so far is in cells and animals.

quick.overview:
Cycloastragenol is the sugar-free form of astragaloside IV, a compound from astragalus root. People take it as an anti-ageing supplement, hoping slower cellular ageing shows up as younger-looking skin and more vitality.

The idea is that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes, which in turn slows cellular ageing. Cell studies report a moderate rise in telomerase activity and animal models show reduced inflammation. A small human study exists on a related telomerase-activator product, and no trial has measured skin or appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily oral supplement, usually sold as capsules, often as part of a longevity stack alongside other ageing-focused compounds. Users generally describe it as a long-term routine, with any change expected to build gradually over months.
quick.risks: Human safety data are limited and toxicity data are sparse. Telomerase is active in most cancers, so a theoretical concern exists about activating it. The FTC issued a consent order over ageing-reversal advertising for the branded product TA-65. It is sold as a supplement, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Cycloastragenol is marketed as a telomerase activator: the idea is slower cellular ageing, which users hope shows up as a younger look and more vitality. Support so far comes from cell and animal work.

astragalus.summary: The root behind huangqi, a classic Chinese tonic herb taken for immunity and healthy ageing, so you look and feel more vital.

quick.overview:
Astragalus root (huangqi) is a staple tonic herb in traditional Chinese medicine, taken for immune support and healthy ageing. People include it in longevity routines hoping that better general health shows up as a fresher, younger look.

Its polysaccharides, astragalosides and isoflavones are reported to modulate immune signalling and inflammation in cell and animal models, and reviews describe immune, antioxidant and metabolic effects. Human trials are few and small, and none has measured appearance. Astragaloside IV is metabolised to cycloastragenol, which is sold separately.
quick.how: It is used as a tea, powder, tincture or capsule, and is common in longevity and immune-support stacks. It is typically taken daily over long periods, as a general tonic rather than something with a quick visible result.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states the toxic constituents of other Astragalus species were not found in the species used in supplements, though those other species are toxic to livestock. Human adverse-effect data are not well covered, and chemical analyses note product quality and adulteration issues. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Astragalus root is a classic Chinese tonic taken for immunity and vitality, and longevity enthusiasts include it in stacks aimed at ageing well. The idea is better general health, which shows as a healthier, younger look; research is mostly in the lab.

gynostemma-pentaphyllum-jiaogulan.summary: A sweet adaptogen tea vine with ginseng-like saponins, used in longevity routines for stress resilience and healthier-looking ageing.

quick.overview:
Jiaogulan, or five-leaf ginseng, is a climbing vine whose leaves are brewed as a sweet tea and sold as an adaptogen. People use it hoping that better stress resilience and general health carry through to healthier-looking skin as they age.

Its leaves contain gypenosides, some chemically identical to ginseng saponins. Lab studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and small preliminary human trials have looked at blood sugar and weight. No trial has measured appearance.
quick.how: Most people drink it as a daily tea, though extracts and capsules are also sold. It is used as a general long-term wellness herb, often alongside other adaptogens, and results are described as gradual if noticed at all.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states there is no information on human toxicity, with toxicity data only from in vitro work. In the EU it is regulated as a novel food. It is sold as a supplement elsewhere.

angle.text: Jiaogulan tea and extracts are used as a ginseng-like adaptogen in longevity routines. Users link lower stress load and better general health with ageing well and healthier-looking skin; research is mostly lab-based.

schisandra-chinensis.summary: The five-flavour berry of Chinese and Russian tonic tradition, taken as an antioxidant and liver-support adaptogen for healthier ageing.

quick.overview:
Schisandra is a vine whose red berries are used as a tonic in Chinese, Korean and Russian traditions. People take the extract as an adaptogen with antioxidant and liver-support properties, hoping better resilience and health show up as healthier-looking skin.

Its lignans, such as schisandrin, are reported in cell and animal studies to act on inflammatory and metabolic signalling. A 2008 review summarises Russian research on it as a tonic and stimulant. Human trials are small, often of multi-herb formulas, and none has measured appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as an extract, capsule or powder, and the berries are also made into a Korean cordial drink. It is used as a daily tonic within longevity or adaptogen routines, often combined with other herbs.
quick.risks: Safety and interaction data are not well covered in the sources reviewed. Product identity can vary because S. chinensis and S. sphenanthera are different species. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Schisandra berry extract is taken as an adaptogen in longevity circles for its antioxidant and liver-support properties. The link to looks is general healthy ageing and healthier-looking skin; studies are lab-based.

rhodiola-rosea.summary: The Arctic adaptogen root taken for stress and fatigue, so you recover better and keep training, which feeds a fitter, fresher look.

quick.overview:
Rhodiola rosea is an Arctic and mountain succulent whose root is sold as an adaptogen for stress, fatigue and stamina. People use it to stay energised and recover, which supports more consistent training and a fitter, fresher appearance.

Its rosavins and salidroside are reported in cell and animal studies to have antioxidant, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory activity. A 2010 review summarised its clinical efficacy, while a 2012 European Medicines Agency report described the published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. Some forum posts discuss hormone effects, but no study cited tests that.
quick.how: It is taken as a standardised root extract in capsules, usually in the morning around work or training. Users generally report noticing effects on fatigue over days to a few weeks, and combine it with other adaptogens and sleep and recovery habits.
quick.risks: FDA has issued warning letters over unapproved health claims. The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II because wild populations are overharvested, and products can be adulterated. Human adverse effects are not well covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Rhodiola is taken as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue: less fatigue means better energy and training capacity, which supports a fitter, fresher look. Human trials on fatigue vary in quality.

eleutherococcus-siberian-ginseng.summary: A thorny Asian shrub root taken as a stress-and-fatigue adaptogen, so a calmer stress response shows in your skin and general look.

quick.overview:
Eleuthero, or Siberian ginseng, is the root of a thorny East Asian shrub used in Russian and Chinese herbal traditions as a tonic. People take it as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue, with some believing a calmer stress response shows in fresher skin and a better overall look.

Extracts contain eleutherosides, lignans and coumarins, and lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-fatigue effects. Published reviews describe the human evidence as limited and mixed, and no trial has tested it for skin or looks. It is not a true ginseng.
quick.how: It is taken as an extract, capsule or tea, usually in the daytime as a general tonic. Users combine it with other recovery and stress-management habits and expect effects over weeks, not days.
quick.risks: Reference summaries list cautions for people with high blood pressure, heart or sleep conditions, and in pregnancy, plus an interaction with digoxin. High intake has been linked to irritability and insomnia. Commercial products vary in content between brands. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Eleuthero is used as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue: a lower stress load is believed to show up as fresher skin and a better general look. Human evidence on stress is limited and mixed.

rhaponticum-carthamoides-maral-root.summary: A Siberian herb rich in ecdysteroids, sold to lifters for muscle, recovery and stress resistance.

quick.overview:
Maral root is a Siberian alpine herb whose roots contain large amounts of 20-hydroxyecdysone, an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in insects. Lifters take it hoping for faster recovery, better protein synthesis and more muscle mass, and it is also used as an adaptogen.

The muscle claim rests on its ecdysteroid content. Published literature on the plant is mostly chemistry and laboratory work, including antioxidant and other activities, and the sources reviewed contain no human trial of it for muscle or appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as an extract or powder in capsules, usually alongside resistance training and often stacked with other muscle or adaptogen supplements. Users generally run it for several weeks while judging gym recovery and progress.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement, and products can be confused with Rheum rhaponticum, a different plant, so the label species matters.

angle.text: Maral root is sold to lifters as an ecdysteroid-rich herb: the ecdysteroids are claimed to support protein synthesis and recovery, leading to more muscle. The muscle claims rest on animal data and user reports.

ganoderma-lucidum-reishi-lingzhi.summary: A traditional East Asian medicinal mushroom taken as tea or extract for immunity, calm and sleep, so you rest better and look fresher.

quick.overview:
Reishi or lingzhi is a woody mushroom used for over two thousand years in East Asian medicine. People take it for immunity, relaxation and sleep, hoping better rest and lower stress show up as a fresher look and better skin.

Polysaccharides and triterpenes are thought to be the active constituents, with immune-modulating and antioxidant effects reported in cell and animal studies. A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no good clinical evidence for cardiovascular or other medical uses owing to poor-quality research, and no trial has tested it for appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as tea, extract or capsules, often in the evening for winding down, or daily as an immune tonic. Users treat it as a long-term routine alongside sleep and recovery habits.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements. Product identity varies: DNA testing found many items labelled G. lucidum contained other species. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Reishi is taken as tea or extract for immunity, stress and sleep: calmer evenings and better rest are hoped to show up as a fresher look and better skin. Clinical research on sleep and immunity is limited.

royal-jelly.summary: Bee-larvae food sold as a supplement and cosmetic ingredient for skin quality and a youthful look.

quick.overview:
Royal jelly is the secretion nurse bees feed to queen larvae. It is sold as a supplement and used in cosmetics, promoted for vitality, smoother skin and a younger look.

It contains protein, sugars, lipids including 10-HDA and B vitamins, and proponents credit it with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. In bees, its proteins drive queen development. The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support human health benefits, and no trial has measured appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as capsules, fresh or freeze-dried jelly, or blended with honey, and it also appears in creams and serums. Users take it as a daily routine over weeks, often alongside other skin supplements.
quick.risks: Allergic reactions from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis have been reported, with higher risk in people with allergies. It is sold as a supplement, and the FDA has acted against unsupported health claims.

angle.text: Royal jelly is taken as a supplement and used in cosmetics for smoother, younger-looking skin, based on its bee-derived nutrients and proteins. EFSA reviewed the human health claims in 2011 and found no support.

maritime-pine-bark-extract-pycnogenol.summary: A pine-bark polyphenol antioxidant taken for skin elasticity, hydration and melasma, aiming at more even, younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Pycnogenol is a branded extract of French maritime pine bark, rich in procyanidins. People take it as an antioxidant for skin elasticity, hydration and pigmentation such as melasma, aiming at more even, younger-looking skin.

Lab studies report free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes involved in breaking down skin structure, by its metabolites, which is the basis for the skin-ageing interest. A Cochrane review updated in 2020 found insufficient evidence of efficacy for the conditions it examined, such as asthma, ADHD and blood pressure. The sources reviewed hold no skin or melasma trial.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily oral capsule, often as part of a skin or antioxidant routine alongside sunscreen and topical care. Skin changes, if any, are expected over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Safety is not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not a drug.

angle.text: Pycnogenol is taken as a procyanidin antioxidant: less oxidative skin damage and enzyme breakdown of skin structure are meant to give more even, younger-looking skin and help with melasma. The link comes from lab work.

grape-seed-extract.summary: A grape-derived procyanidin antioxidant taken for skin and ageing, which some forum users also use as an aromatase inhibitor.

quick.overview:
Grape seed extract is a supplement made from grape seeds, rich in procyanidin polyphenols. People take it as an antioxidant for healthier, younger-looking skin, and some forum users add it hoping to lower estrogen via aromatase inhibition.

Procyanidins scavenge free radicals in lab tests, and cell studies show inhibition of aromatase and digestive enzymes. Human trials are small and have looked at blood pressure, lipids, vascular stiffness and exercise rather than appearance. Effects on estrogen in humans have not been published.
quick.how: It is taken as daily capsules, and it also appears as an ingredient in topical skin products. Users add it to skin or antioxidant routines and generally give it weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported effects are mild, such as stomach upset and headache, according to secondary sources, with possible interactions with anticoagulants. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US.

angle.text: Grape seed extract is taken as a polyphenol antioxidant: less oxidative damage is meant to leave skin healthier and younger-looking, and some forum users also use it as an aromatase inhibitor to lower estrogen. The case comes from lab data.

genistein.summary: A soy phytoestrogen used for skin ageing, acting on estrogen receptors in skin to support a younger-looking complexion.

quick.overview:
Genistein is the main isoflavone in soy, a plant compound that resembles estrogen. People consider it for skin ageing, expecting its phytoestrogen and antioxidant activity to support collagen and a younger-looking complexion.

It binds estrogen receptors, more strongly to the beta subtype in lab assays, and inhibits tyrosine kinases in laboratory tests. It has been studied for heart, bone and cancer research, and no trial has tested it for skin or cosmetic outcomes. Oral bioavailability is described as low.
quick.how: It is eaten through soy foods or taken as an isoflavone supplement, and discussed in topical form for skin. Users treat it as a long-term daily addition to a skin or ageing routine.
quick.risks: Animal studies show estrogen-related effects, while secondary sources describe human hormone data as largely reassuring. It is a food component and supplement rather than an approved drug.

angle.text: Genistein is a soy isoflavone that users consider for skin ageing, since phytoestrogens act on estrogen receptors in skin and are thought to support collagen. It has been studied for heart, bone and cancer, not for skin.

diosmin.summary: A citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling that some try for fluid retention and puffiness, including in the face.

quick.overview:
Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used to treat chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and leg swelling, usually with hesperidin. People try it hoping to reduce fluid pooling and puffiness elsewhere, including the face, and it appears in bruise and swelling supplements.

It is reported to raise venous tone, reduce capillary permeability and dampen inflammation after conversion to diosmetin, which is how it helps leg swelling. It is a prescription medicine in parts of Europe and a supplement in the US. No trial has tested it for facial puffiness.
quick.how: It is taken as an oral tablet or capsule, often as a micronised blend with hesperidin, daily over weeks. Bruise-support products combine it with arnica, bromelain and vitamin C.
quick.risks: Product labels mention mild stomach upset, nausea and rash, and rarely bleeding or hypersensitivity. Combination bruise products carry additional warnings for their other ingredients.

angle.text: Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling, and some users try it hoping that better vein and lymph flow means less fluid pooling and less puffiness in the face. Its use for venous swelling is studied.

krill-oil.summary: A phospholipid-bound omega-3 supplement that raises blood EPA and DHA, taken for calmer, healthier skin.

quick.overview:
Krill oil is an omega-3 supplement from Antarctic krill, with EPA and DHA carried on phospholipids and the carotenoid astaxanthin alongside. People take it for skin and general health, hoping less inflammation and a better skin barrier give calmer, healthier skin.

Several small trials report that it raises blood EPA and DHA about as well as fish oil, and the claimed advantage is better uptake. It is discussed for skin and inflammation, but no study has tested it for appearance. Fish oil has the larger outcome evidence base.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily softgel with a meal, usually as part of a general skin and health routine. Omega-3 changes build over weeks, and users often pair it with other skin-care habits.
quick.risks: Being crustacean-derived, it is not suited to shellfish-free diets. Krill research is newer and smaller than fish oil research, and harvest is regulated by CCAMLR.

angle.text: Krill oil is taken as a phospholipid-bound omega-3 source with astaxanthin: higher blood EPA and DHA are meant to lower inflammation and support the skin barrier, for calmer skin. It raises blood omega-3 in studies; skin effects are untested.

sodium-beta-hydroxybutyrate-bhb-salts.summary: Ketone-salt supplements that raise blood ketones, taken on low-carb diets for appetite, energy and a leaner body.

quick.overview:
BHB salts are supplements that bind the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate to minerals such as sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium. People on low-carb diets use them hoping raised ketones ease appetite and energy dips and help them get leaner.

BHB is the main ketone body the liver makes during fasting and low-carb eating, and the salts supply it directly, raising blood BHB without fasting. Research is limited to small physiology studies, and fat loss from the salts has not been tested in published trials found here. Most products are racemic, so only about half is the form the body uses.
quick.how: They are mixed as a powder drink or taken as capsules, usually alongside a ketogenic or low-carb diet or around fasting. Users take them for appetite and energy during the adaptation period.
quick.risks: The salts add a mineral load such as sodium and slightly raise blood pH. Long-term safety data in healthy dieters are limited.

angle.text: BHB salts are used by people on low-carb diets who hope raised blood ketones ease appetite and shift energy toward a leaner body. They do raise blood BHB; effects on fat loss have not been tested.

ketone-monoester-r-1-3-butanediol-ester.summary: The most-studied ketone drink, which quickly raises blood ketones and lowered appetite hormones in one study, used for appetite control and leanness.

quick.overview:
The ketone monoester is a drink that quickly raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate. It was developed at the NIH and sold under brands such as KetoneAid, and people use it for appetite control and fat loss on the way to a leaner body.

It is broken down into ketone bodies the body can use as fuel, raising blood ketones without fasting or dieting. It is the best-studied exogenous ketone, with human studies on kinetics, endurance and appetite, including one report of lower ghrelin and appetite. Fat loss and appearance have not been tested in published trials found here.
quick.how: It is drunk as a liquid, often around training or between meals to blunt hunger, and used alongside a low-carb or calorie-controlled diet.
quick.risks: The 2012 study reported on tolerability in healthy adults. Long-term effects in healthy dieters are not established.

angle.text: The ketone monoester drink raises blood ketones quickly, and the appearance interest is appetite control: one study found lower appetite hormones, which could help you eat less and get leaner. Fat-loss trial results are not published.

glyceryl-tris-3-hydroxybutyrate.summary: A ketone triglyceride (3GHB) that releases beta-hydroxybutyrate, discussed as a way to raise ketones for appetite and fat loss.

quick.overview:
Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate is a water-soluble oil in which glycerol carries three beta-hydroxybutyrate groups. In ketone-supplement circles it is discussed as a way to raise blood ketones, with appetite control and fat loss as the hoped-for outcome.

After ingestion the ester groups are expected to be cleaved, releasing beta-hydroxybutyrate and glycerol into circulation where tissues can burn the ketone. The human studies registered for it are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers, and no efficacy trials for fat loss or appearance appear in the sources.
quick.how: It is discussed as an oral ketone supplement used alongside low-carb or fasting routines. It remains less common than ketone salts or esters, and mostly appears in research and novel-food discussions.
quick.risks: A 2025 toxicology package sponsored for novel-food use reported no genotoxicity and no adverse effects in a 90-day rat study. Human safety data are limited, and it is the subject of a pending EU novel-food application, not an authorization.

angle.text: This ketone triglyceride (3GHB) releases beta-hydroxybutyrate and is discussed in ketone-supplement circles as a way to raise ketones, with appetite and fat loss as the hoped-for outcome. Human work so far is pharmacokinetic studies.

r-1-3-butanediol.summary: A diol the body converts into the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate, used in ketone supplements for appetite and leanness.

quick.overview:
R-1,3-butanediol is the (R) form of a four-carbon diol that the body converts into beta-hydroxybutyrate. It appears in the exogenous ketone field as a precursor and as a component of some ketone esters, used with appetite control and fat loss in mind.

Wikipedia's ketone ester article states it raises blood ketones, by about 60 percent relative to the monoester, and notes that exogenous ketones lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing it for fat loss or appearance.
quick.how: It is used as a liquid or as an ingredient in ketone drinks, typically alongside low-carb eating or fasting. It is not the same as 1,4-butanediol, which converts to GHB.
quick.risks: 1,3-butanediol is recognized by the US FDA as a safe food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712), per Wikipedia. Pure chemical hazard notes include eye irritation. A study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.

angle.text: R-1,3-butanediol is converted to beta-hydroxybutyrate and raises blood ketones, with lower hunger and fat loss as the hoped-for payoff. Human evidence for fat loss or appearance has not been established.

alanyl-glutamine.summary: A stable glutamine dipeptide that lifters consider for recovery and muscle retention; its research is in hospital nutrition.

quick.overview:
Alanyl-glutamine is a synthetic dipeptide of alanine and glutamine, made so glutamine can be given in a stable, water-soluble form. Some lifters consider it for muscle recovery and holding on to muscle.

Given intravenously, the dipeptide supplies glutamine to tissues. A 1989 Lancet trial of 12 patients after colorectal surgery examined muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance, and later research covered surgery, trauma, critical illness and gut disease. Results vary, including a randomized study that found no benefit in autologous transplant patients. No trials target muscle growth or appearance in healthy people.
quick.how: Lifters use it as a powder mixed into drinks, typically around training, in the same slot as ordinary glutamine. Clinical use is as part of hospital nutrition.
quick.risks: Reported trials are in hospital patients and results vary. No safety data from healthy-lifter use appear in the reference material.

angle.text: Alanyl-glutamine is a stable glutamine dipeptide that some lifters consider for faster recovery and keeping more muscle. Its research is in hospital nutrition, such as muscle glutamine loss after surgery.

glutamine.summary: The most abundant amino acid in blood, taken as a recovery supplement so you can train harder and hold more muscle.

quick.overview:
Glutamine is a conditionally essential amino acid that the body makes in large amounts, mostly in muscle. Lifters take it as a recovery supplement, hoping to recover faster, train more and keep more muscle.

It is a protein building block, a nitrogen carrier between organs and a fuel for gut-lining and immune cells, and it is used to make glutathione. The documented clinical uses are medical: a prescription form was approved by the US FDA in 2017 for sickle cell disease, and it is used in some hospital nutrition settings, where evidence is described as low quality. No trials in the reference material test it for muscle gain in healthy lifters.
quick.how: It is taken as a powder mixed into drinks, often around training and in combination body-composition products. Users treat it as part of a recovery stack.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes supplemental glutamine as considered safe in adults, with an observed safe level of 14 g/day in healthy adults, and notes adverse effects in people on home parenteral nutrition or with liver abnormalities. Side effects of the prescription form include constipation, nausea, headache and abdominal pain.

angle.text: Glutamine is taken by lifters as a recovery supplement: faster recovery means more and harder training, and so more muscle. Its clinical evidence is in medical settings such as illness and injury.
